review.material: The author-uploaded 1972 reprint text, pp. 125–134, was read.
review.limitations: Figures were not reliably available; the proceedings copy was not checked.

evidence.description: James Gips’s public author upload; explicitly the Best Computer Papers reprint, not the proceedings pagination.

sections.title: What it is about
sections.text: Stiny and Gips specify families of geometric artworks through shape-generating rules and separate instructions for material realization.

sections.title: Premise
sections.text: A generative specification can describe a class independently of any one finished artwork.

sections.title: The formal machinery
sections.text: The reprint defines a grammar with terminals, markers, rules and an initial shape, then adds selection rules, painting instructions and a limiting canvas shape.

sections.title: The demonstration
sections.text: The Urform example links recursive shape generation with colouring based on level-defined regions. Sculpture extends the arrangement to three dimensions.

sections.title: Proposed conclusion
sections.text: Artists can choose relationships and determine their consequences algorithmically. The aesthetic discussion proposes relating compact specifications to visual complexity.

sections.title: Important historical boundary
sections.text: This early definition restricts terminal erasure. It should not be substituted unchanged for later, more general shape arithmetic. No controlled test of artistic quality is reported.

sections.title: How to read it
sections.text: Separate generating geometry, selecting outcomes and specifying materials. Keep the inspected reprint’s pages distinct from the proceedings citation.
